topics.title: All multiplication facts to 10×10: Recall facts for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10; use known facts to find related facts

questions.stem: Will the answer to \(\text{even} \times \text{even}\) be odd or even?
questions.hint: Test two simple examples of even × even and check whether the results end in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) or an odd digit (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

keyPoints.note: Try two small number examples to verify the parity rule.

steps.explain: Choose a first pair of small numbers that match \(\text{even} \times \text{even}\) and calculate the result.
Check the last digit of the first result to see if it is even or odd. It is even.
Test a second pair of numbers to confirm the pattern always holds.
Both tests confirm the general rule: \(\text{even} \times \text{even}\) is always even.

questions.stem: Will the answer to \(\text{odd} \times \text{odd}\) be odd or even?
questions.hint: Test two simple examples of odd × odd and check whether the results end in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) or an odd digit (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

keyPoints.note: Try two small number examples to verify the parity rule.

steps.explain: Choose a first pair of small numbers that match \(\text{odd} \times \text{odd}\) and calculate the result.
Check the last digit of the first result to see if it is even or odd. It is odd.
Test a second pair of numbers to confirm the pattern always holds.
Both tests confirm the general rule: \(\text{odd} \times \text{odd}\) is always odd.

questions.stem: Will the answer to \(\text{even} \times \text{odd}\) be odd or even?
questions.hint: Test two simple examples of even × odd and check whether the results end in an even digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) or an odd digit (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).

keyPoints.note: Try two small number examples to verify the parity rule.

steps.explain: Choose a first pair of small numbers that match \(\text{even} \times \text{odd}\) and calculate the result.
Check the last digit of the first result to see if it is even or odd. It is even.
Test a second pair of numbers to confirm the pattern always holds.
Both tests confirm the general rule: \(\text{even} \times \text{odd}\) is always even.

topics.title: Area model: Use the structure of the area model to represent multiplication and division
Factors and multiples: Identify factors of numbers; investigate number sequences of related multiples
Multiples of 10: Operate with multiples of 10 using known number facts and strategies
All division facts to 10×10: Recall division facts for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10; inverse operations

questions.stem: In this multiplication square, each inside number is the product of its row header and column header. What number belongs in the bottom-right square (?)?
questions.hint: Find a common factor of 15 and 12 for the top-row header, then divide to find the column headers and the bottom-row header.

keyPoints.note: Each inside cell equals its row header multiplied by its column header.
Use common factors of 15 and 12, and of 15 and 20, to unlock all four headers.

steps.explain: Look at the top row: \(15\) and \(12\) share the common factor \(3\). Place \(3\) as the top-row header.

topics.title: Word problems: Represent and solve word problems with number sentences involving multiplication or division

questions.stem: Using each of the digits \(5, 8,\) and \(4\) once, and using addition or multiplication, what is the largest number you can make?
questions.hint: Multiplying a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number beats adding or multiplying three 1-digit numbers. Compare 8 × 54 and 5 × 84 carefully!

keyPoints.note: Use 5, 8, and 4 once each; you can combine two digits into a 2-digit number.
Test the top multiplication combinations: 8 × 54 and 5 × 84.

steps.explain: Compare multiplying three 1-digit numbers against multiplying a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number. Making a 2-digit number gives a much larger product.

steps.explain: Test putting the largest digit \(8\) as the tens digit of the 2-digit number: \(5 \times 84\).
